_comment: Bob keeps a TO-DO list and it never gets shorter (Bk1 ch2, ch12, ch13, ch21). Ours is the research backlog, rendered the way Guppy reports his: a bracketed count, divided into categories. Add freely; that's the joke.

items.text: Books restored and the cache guarded
items.note: The five ebooks were deleted by a commit-splitting script that ran rm -rf on directories before restoring them from git archive — books/ is gitignored, so nothing came back but .gitkeep. It went unnoticed for hours because .cache/corpus.json survived and every build and test kept passing. Restored from backup 11 Aug 2026. `make corpus` now refuses to overwrite the cache when any book parses to fewer chapters than it already holds, and refuses an empty books/ rather than treating it as an empty corpus; --force overrides. The restored book 1 is the 2016 EPUB rather than the MOBI, which needed a third header detector — see the chapter-parsing notes.

items.text: Browser test harness moved into the repo
items.note: Lived in a scratch directory, so it didn't survive a session and its record-count assertions went stale unnoticed — it asserted 86 records for a whole session after the 87th landed. Now tests/ behind `make test`, run against the shipped dist/index.html rather than the template. Expectations are derived from data/*.json instead of hardcoded. Its first run found two live bugs: build.py's ORDER whitelist was silently dropping `alias` and `priorClaim`, so the HAS LEAD chip matched nothing and Will's "/ Riker" never rendered. Includes a golden-master snapshot of 95 states, so the console restructure can be verified by diff.

items.text: Star chart: label decluttering and the two judgement calls
items.note:
Both open questions turned out to have measurable answers rather than aesthetic ones.

The backdrop was cut from magnitude 6 to 5.5, which is where the console's own brightness ramp bottoms out: alpha is (7.0 - m) / 5.2 clamped at 0.30, so every star fainter than 5.44 rendered at the same alpha and the same 1.1px square. The 2,065 dropped were not carrying magnitude, they were uniform speckle over the systems, and 37KB of page weight. data/skyfield.json keeps magnitude_limit 6.0 as the record of the extract and gains display_limit 5.5 as what the build ships; the page states its own limit from the data. backdrop.test.js asserts a star at 6.0 would render identically to one at 5.5, so the justification fails loudly if anyone retunes the ramp.

The glow was cut too far, and the reasoning had two knobs mixed together. Radius controls whether neighbours merge — that was the blob problem and it stays at 2.6x. Opacity controls nothing about the core, which is drawn opaque over the glow, so everything inside offset 38.5% is never seen. Out where the gradient is visible it reached the star's edge at 0.11 alpha, dimmer than the faintest backdrop star at the 0.30 floor. Stops moved to .55/.34 at 0/40%, which clears the floor without spreading.

The labels: the note named Gliese 54, Zeta Tucanae and Gliese 877, but the measurement at the default camera found p Eridani and Zeta Tucanae — the note had drifted. Four candidate positions became eight directions across three rings, and coverage went from 73.1% to 86.3% over 24 camera and viewport combinations, worst case 9 of 20 up to 14. Reach is guarded rather than capped: a name may go as far as it likes provided it stays nearer its own dot than anyone else's, measured at the anchor corner. A dropped name is honestly absent; a drifted one is the chart stating something false.

items.text: Galaxy scale view — later
items.note: Everything the Bobs reach fits inside 48.8 ly; the galaxy is ~100,000 ly across, so at that scale the whole story is smaller than a pixel. That's the point of it rather than an obstacle — but any Milky Way rendering is an artist's impression, so it belongs in the decoration bucket, clearly marked. Defer until the local chart is finished.

items.text: Console restructured around a register list
items.note: Every view used to be hardcoded: five tab buttons in the markup, a ternary chain in render(), and state.view special cases in the dossier, the paint step and the resize handler. Adding a sixth register meant editing all of them. Now REGISTERS drives all five, and a new view is one entry plus one render function. Done as a golden-master refactor — the 95-state snapshot was byte-identical before and after, so nothing rendered differently. tests/registers.test.js adds a synthetic register at runtime and checks every hook fires, so the next state.view special case will fail the build rather than rot quietly.

items.text: Chase the 12 remaining dropped-source leads through the text
items.note: Twelve left, all from the fandom wiki; the eighteen from Taylor's tree were settled by the genealogy printed in book 2. The claim isn't drawn, but it says where to look. Anything the books confirm gets promoted; anything they contradict is worth writing up.

items.text: Marcus — parentage
items.note: Ten POV chapters across books 3 and 4, and no source anywhere names who built him. The last major POV character still unaccounted for.

items.text: Thor, Jeffrey, Milton, Zeke — parentage
items.note: Jeffrey, Milton and Zeke have a citation for their deaths at 82 Eridani. Nothing names who made them.

items.text: Resolve the Hector collision
items.note: A third-generation Hector lost at 82 Eridani and an ~18th-generation Hector emailing Bill in 2343. Either the naming convention broke down or they're two Bobs. Currently two records and the only standing validator warning.

items.text: Verne — parentage beyond the appendix
items.note: Settled as Bill's clone by the Cast of Characters. The narrative only ever put him on Loki's crew at 82 Eridani, which was suggestive and never stated. Worth a look for a narrative confirmation.

items.text: Light biographical sweep, name by name
items.note: Rebuild born, vessel and designation from the text rather than from the sources we dropped. 17 birth dates, 3 vessels and 43 generation numbers came out in the sweep; some are certainly recoverable by reading around each name.

items.text: Systems: check origin and visited the same way
items.note:
Done. Both fields are swept, and the map is the receipt: nine of the twenty-two systems had no record pointing at them when this was raised, and two do now. The two are Tau Ceti and Kappa Ceti, which have nought scenes and no narrator and sit in the file because the books name them as distances rather than as destinations. Starfleet's purged location data (Bk4 ch32) turned out not to cost anything here.

The obvious method was wrong, which is the finding worth keeping. A Bob who narrates a chapter set at a star was not necessarily at that star: Bill narrates chapters headed Gliese 54, 82 Eridani, Delta Pavonis, Gamma Pavonis and Sol, and each one says in its own prose that he is working drones from Epsilon Eridani, or visiting Claude's VR, or hosting the moot, or popping into Mack's. Run mechanically, the sweep would have added five star systems to the record of the Bob who never leaves home. So `visited` now has a definition in the schema — the Bob's matrix was there — and a manny or a VR session driven over SCUT does not count, which is the same rule that stops a moot from placing every Bob at Epsilon Eridani. Twenty-one candidate pairs came out of the header pass; six were rejected on reading, and four more are left alone because the books show a manny and never say where the matrix is.

Two values were simply wrong. Steve was recorded at Sol; Bk3 ch44 has Jacques arriving at HIP 84051 and spending a month reading Steve's survey of it. Xavier Charles was recorded at Gamma Pavonis; Bk5 ch26 has him as the resident Bob on Trantor, which is one of the systems the map was showing hollow.

Ten records that had no citation of any kind now have one, and eight of those had nothing written on them at all: Owen, Jack and Isaac arriving as the colony-ship Bobs at 82 Eridani; Sam bringing Exodus-3 in to the Vulcan/Romulus L4 point; Monty as the colony transport at Poseidon; Harvey as the Bob-in-residence on Earth; Hank posted at p Eridani; Benny on the lunar terraforming crew; plus Linus, Bashful, Claude and Rudy, who had citations but no prose.

Two things fell out that the sweep was not looking for. Bk3 ch21 states Isaac's parentage outright — one of Bart's early clones, senior even to Oliver — which agrees with his HIC71683 designation and promotes him from tier C to tier T. And Bk3 ch74 calls Harvey a tenth-generation Bob, which is storable `gen` because he has no parent for the tree to count down from. Bk2 ch13 also gives Bashful, Dopey, Sleepy and Hungry an origin in a single sentence: Mario builds all four at Gliese 54. Mario's second cohort — Hal, Claude, Jacques — was almost certainly built there too, a chapter later, but the books do not name them in the sentence that says so, and that is the difference between a record and a guess.

The other half of the pair is `scenes` and `povs` in systems.json, which are header-derived and stay that way: they index where the story happens and who tells it. The dossier labelled that NARRATED FROM HERE, which claims a presence the data cannot support, and it printed the list ungated so a reader on book one was told Will's name two books before he stops being Riker. Both fixed. Checking the derivation rather than the values also turned up two counting errors: Linus's Epsilon Indi chapter was filed under Epsilon Eridani, and two of Icarus's book-5 chapters were counted at Alpha Centauri because a wormhole destination is named Centaurvania.

Two year ranges moved with those corrections — Alpha Centauri's last year was 2329, which was the Centaurvania chapter, and Epsilon Indi's first was 2190, which was Linus's chapter being counted elsewhere. Two more are left alone and are worth a look by whoever next touches the file: 82 Eridani says its last year is 2336 and Delta Eridani says 2233, and no chapter set in either system carries those dates. They may be curated from something other than chapter headers, which is precisely the thing this sweep learned not to assume in the other direction.

items.text: Back matter: book 4 has an appendix too, and nobody had read it
items.note: Answered, and the assumption in the question was wrong. Book 4 carries the same three appendices as book 2 — List of Acronyms, Cast of Characters and Genealogy — reprinted with GUPPI added to the acronyms and everything else identical to the line. Books 1, 3 and 5 have none. More to the point, none of it was in the corpus: the parser needs a POV and a date to recognise a chapter, back matter has neither, so every automated sweep this project has ever run walked straight past it. Now parsed as appendix entries numbered after the narrative, so a citation can't collide with a chapter number, and the manifest counts chapters and appendices separately so the count that citations depend on stays a tripwire.

items.text: Second pass on the moot scenes for later generations
items.note:
Done, and it found two Bobs the register did not have: Wally, who interrupts the war-planning moot in Bk2 ch39 to ask whether they had actually voted on the war, and Ben, named from the crowd at the Bk2 ch66 moot as one of the new batch of dreadnaughts. Both are tier C — a name, a chapter, and no ancestor anywhere. Ben is not the Ben Hendricks who sits on the UFS council in Bk4 ch45; that one is human and a hundred and twenty-six years later, and the disambiguation lives here rather than on the record because a book-2-safe note may not cite book 4 — the validator says so, and it said so the moment it was tried. Tony, whom the first pass did find, was carrying a note about a moot with no citation to it; he is Bk2 ch74, which also drops his spoil from 3 to 2, since everything his note draws on happens in book 2.

The reason written down for re-sweeping was wrong. The six chapters the parser recovered are the appendices of books 2 and 4, and an appendix contains no moot. The corpus the first pass read is, for this purpose, the corpus the second pass read — so what changed was the method, not the evidence. The first pass found Tony, who has a dialogue tag on his line, and missed Wally and Ben in chapters it must have had open. Wally is introduced by being interrupted and by stepping forward; Ben by being nodded at. A sweep for who speaks finds the first and not the others.

Four modalities this time, deliberately different from each other rather than four spellings of one idea: every capitalised token in the moot chapters diffed against the register; every name in a speech or address position; every name in a vocative; and every name-run of three or more. The address pass is the one that earned its keep — it is the only one that catches a Bob who is gestured at rather than quoted. A proper name was identified by never appearing lower-case anywhere in 357 chapters, which is cheaper and better than any stopword list, and it is what let the run stay readable enough to check by hand.

The chapter set was wrong twice. This project's note said 55 moot chapters; the first run here said 56, because the pattern was written \bmoot\b and there are six chapters that only ever say moots — Bk3 ch14, Bk3 ch74, Bk4 ch62, Bk5 ch22, Bk5 ch38 and Bk5 ch72, one of which is named for a moot in its own chapter title. The real figure is 62. Making the same class of mistake in the same hour as writing the lesson down is worth recording: those six added no Bobs, so nothing was lost, but nothing about the method guaranteed that. Their unfamiliar names are Bridget's dinner-party friends on Vulcan, two humans on Earth, and the Quinlan and human regulars already accounted for.

The null results are worth as much as the finds, because they are what makes 'exhausted' mean something this time. Every other unfamiliar name at a moot resolves to a non-Bob: Henry Roberts is the Australian probe's replicant and says outright he does not replicate; Bridget, Hannah Turnbull and Steven Gilligan are human guests; Theresa Sykorski and Anec are Quinlan; Charlie is Bob's Deltan android per the Cast of Characters, and the one line at Delta Pavonis that seems to give the name to somebody else is a single unattributed tag with nothing else behind it, which is a smaller thing than the Hector collision and not worth a second record. Hersch and Icky are Herschel and Icarus, Marv is Marvin, Jock is what the Pav call Jacques, Scotty and Spock are the jokes they look like, and Pacino is Al. No moot names a generation number for anybody; the generation talk in those chapters is all in aggregate — eight to ten deep at book 2, fifteen to twenty by book 4, some past twenty.

items.text: Bestiary built
items.note: Nine creatures in data/bestiary.json, with its own register and an illustration pipeline. The inherited candidate list was mostly wrong — five of eight entries did not survive checking against the text: landers is Dr. Landers, spits is a human faction, boojums are Quinlan drones, hexghi is the Deltan word for a family group, and snarks are Quinlans, who are people. It also missed dragons entirely, at 191 mentions the most-discussed animal in the series. Still to do: a second pass for Ragnarok and Heaven's River river life, and the 'contested sapience' cases the books deliberately leave open.

items.text: Peoples and polities built
items.note: Five species and nine polities in data/peoples.json, with its own register. Provenance is graded differently from the tree — species and governments have no parents — so what's recorded is whether the books state a thing or leave it open. Acronyms carry an expansion only where a character expands it on the page: USE is the United States of Eurasia, VEHEMENT keeps Butterworth's own hedge, and FAITH has none because the books never give one. A name may be a people or fauna and never both; validate.py checks the two files against each other. Still to do: the Arcadians and Zjentfen, both single mentions; the human colony governments on Vulcan, Romulus, Poseidon and Newholme; and the Bob factions, which currently live as a field on bobs.json rather than here.

items.text: Blog posts in Bill's voice
items.note: Done — `data/blog.json` and a peer register at #blog/<id>. Three posts, and the build of it turned up a problem worth recording: two of the three could not be Bill's. A post about appendices, parse failures or provenance rules is written from outside the story, and Bill does not know the books are books. So posts carry a `voice` — bobnet or editor — labelled in the list and in the dossier, the same seam the annotations already draw. The validator fails a bobnet post that says appendix, Taylor, novel or canon, because that drift happens one edit at a time and reads fine each time.

items.text: Images
items.note: Later. Whatever we do has to survive the no-external-requests rule, so anything visual gets inlined. Settled shape: images are payload, never chrome. The shell stays terminal and an opened attachment in a dossier is allowed to be rich — [ATTACHMENT: dragon.plate] and a panel that is clearly the opened file. An empty plate stays 'no file on record', because a Bob with no known parent must never get a handsome illustration to make up for it.

items.text: Illustrate the bestiary
items.note:
Two of nine have art — dragon and kraken, drawn as stroke-only SVG so the console can colour them with currentColor. The rest show a dashed plate with their role mark. Adding one is: draw assets/bestiary/<id>.svg, rebuild. The build refuses art containing a script or an external URL, so the page keeps its promise of zero external requests.

Done — nine of nine, 16 KB of drawing for the whole register, which is the argument for stroke SVG in one number: the single raster concept in ideas/ is 325 KB on disk and about 434 KB once base64'd, so one photograph would cost more than twenty-seven of these on a page that has to open from a file:// double-click.

Two needed a decision rather than a drawing. Leviathan is described only by scale, and a plate cannot show scale without a reference that the survey never recorded beside it — so the composition carries it instead: the body enters past one edge and leaves past the other, and the frame cannot hold the animal. Hydra is the most speculative plate here and says so in its own source; the books name it exactly once with no description, so the drawing reads the name and stops, with the rearmost necks left faint because we do not know how many there are. If the corpus ever describes it, redraw rather than defend it.

One test had to change. It asserted that some creature on the page had no art, which held until every creature had some — then the check for the empty-plate path failed because the path had stopped being exercised, not because it had broken. Coverage that depends on a gap in the data evaporates when the data improves, so the reserved plate is now rendered from a creature that does not exist, the way registers.test.js adds a register at runtime.

items.text: Second pass on peoples: colonies, minor species, Bob factions
items.note:
Done, and the register went from fourteen entries to thirty. Its own inventory in this note was wrong twice, in both directions.

The Arcadians do not exist. Not one occurrence in five books; the name was almost certainly a memory of the Arcadia River, which is one of the four rivers inside Heaven's River. Zjentfen is real but is not a species — Bk2 ch63 has Jacques learning a Pav country's language by parking drones in the shadows of reading clubs, and its inhabitants call themselves Zjentfen and their language Tinozj. It is in as a polity of the Pav, defunct, because the Others stripped that planet.

What the note missed is larger than what it got wrong. The **Roanokians** are a species with 25 mentions, described in detail, and were not in the register at all. And the **dragons** of Jabberwocky are people: the first time anyone asks what to call them the question is whether we have a name for the intelligent species yet. They build towns, keep written records and fight a war of conquest. They were in the bestiary with sapience: none, and moving them out is what this pass is really for. The build caught it — a name may not be filed as both, and the check that refused it was written for exactly this case. Their mention count helped hide it: 191 across two books, but seventeen of those are book 4, where the word means a D&D monster in the Gamers' campaign or the idiom dragon fodder, and the entry's citation pointed at one of the idioms.

The colony governments came out well, with one correction to the premise. Vulcan has a council but the books never name it, and Romulus's colonial polity is not called Romulus — it is **New Jerusalem**, Cranston's, which becomes a democracy after incriminating video forces him out and which is electing FAITH again two books later. **Poseidon Administrative Council** is named in Bk3 ch3 and is the one government in this register the books show being overthrown, with five of its seven councillors captured. **Newholme Council** — locally the Big Heads — issues a military arrest order for Claude and later puts facial recognition into everything, whereupon the entire population spends a week wearing masks of the president. Pangea was already in.

FAITH was wrong and is now corrected: the register had it defunct. It outlives both the state and the planet, runs slates on Romulus, does better than expected, and takes a majority government in book 5. Will names its resurgence and the rise of the Luddies as two wars in the making — the **Luddies** being another entry this pass added, along with the **Ever Onward Society**, the **Pan Galactic Federation** (an alien power the Bobs meet only through an automated station that warns them off and then hands over its own comms protocols), and three of the six Earth powers the register had been leaving out: China, the Australian Federation and the Republic of Africa. Australia matters more than its two mentions suggest — its probe is where Henry Roberts comes from.

The Bob factions came in as their own kind rather than as polities, which needed a third value in `kind`, a rule in validate.py that a faction may not carry a system, a place or an `of`, and a `factionTag` tying each entry to the tag records already carry. The console links both ways now: a record's FACTION opens the entry, and the entry lists its joiners.

One thing left undone on purpose. assets/bestiary/dragon.svg stays where it is, unused: it is a 4:3 side profile labelled survey silhouette, and the peoples register draws 16:10 portraits because a specimen and a portrait make different claims. Carrying the plate across would have made the drawing say what the entry no longer does. The dragons owe a portrait.

Adjacent, and fixed while in there: **floaters** are missing no longer — Jabberwocky's living hydrogen islands, 133 mentions, the thing dragon towns are built on. Howard called them leviathans first, which collides with Poseidon's marine giant, and that is the third name collision this project has recorded after Hector and Surly. The floater has a plate; it took five passes, and the four that failed are written into the file's own comment, because each failed in a different way and the corrections are most of the drawing.

items.text: Cross-register links — make the registers admit the others exist
items.note: Done, and the mechanism turned out to be one already here. A link between registers is just an address — <a href="#chart/82_eridani"> — so it inherits applyHash, which refuses an unknown view and drops a selection the reading position holds back, plus copy-link-address and middle-click, and needs no click handler to stay in step. What links now: a Bob's origin, visited and lost-at into the chart; a system into the fauna and peoples recorded there, which was in the data and never on the page; a creature to the Bob who named it, via a new namedById; and the blog both ways — a post declares what it is about as addresses, and every record reads that same list backwards to show ON THE FEED. One mapping, two directions, so the two cannot disagree. A held target vanishes from a list rather than degrading to its name, because in a list the name is the whole content.

items.text: URL state, so a dossier can actually be linked to
items.note: Done. #<view>/<selection>?q=&f= — hash rather than query string, so it still works when the file is opened by double-clicking it, which has to keep being true after publishing. Arriving on a link skips the six-second boot. An unknown view is refused outright and a selection that no longer resolves is dropped rather than obeyed, so a stale link lands on the right register with nothing selected instead of an empty dossier for a ghost. Every register keeps its selection somewhere different — state.selected, CHART.sel, state.beast, state.people — so selOf() is the only place that knows, and tests/url.test.js walks the whole register list to catch the next one that gets wired into the tab bar and forgotten here. Renaming a register keeps its old links working through VIEW_ALIAS: #lineage/ still resolves and the bar respells itself in place.

items.text: Timeline register — the one axis nothing reads
items.note:
Done, and it needed no data file. Every other register sorts by name, by structure or by how loud a thing is; none of them said what happened when, and the dates were already here — build dates on records, fate citations, first contact on systems, Bill's posts, the failed transfers at 82 Eridani. The timeline is those five put in one column, the same way In Memorium was an axis over bobs.json rather than a new dataset.

Two date parsers were quietly living in the memorium view; there is one now, and it handles both shapes the project uses — a build date like 'Jul 2145' and a citation with the date at its end. A month of zero means only a year was given and sorts ahead of anything dated inside it, rather than pretending to precision.

Three things the build turned up. The original is woken, not built — Bk1 ch2, Landers gives him the date, a hundred and seventeen years after he died — so the verb is conditional on having a parent. The registry's own posts are dated to now and are not events in the story, so only Bill's appear. And a system carries a first contact year with no citation to gate it against, so a place a visible Bob merely passed through could date itself past the last thing the reader has read; places are now bounded by how far the records reach. The span grows with the reading position: 2185 at book one, then 2217, 2257, 2334, 2343.

items.text: Holotank — rich payload, amber chrome
items.note:
Checked against the corpus before writing it down: holotank 34 hits, hologram 22, holographic 8, holoview 1, holosphere 0. Holosphere is the coinage we'd have reached for and it isn't Taylor's word, so that's a bullet dodged. The rule if this ever gets built: the shell stays terminal and the opened file can be rich. Drab file manager, rich document. Tabs, phosphor, Guppy and the bracketed metadata stay exactly as they are; an attachment in the dossier is allowed to be a real picture, labelled as machine-attached media. What it must never do is give a Bob with no known parent a handsome illustrated tree to make up for it. If media ever lands on a Bob record, it goes in the schema AND in build.py's ORDER — that whitelist has already silently eaten two fields.

Surveyed the prior art since. ruguevara/Bobmap is the one to look at — Three.js, TypeScript, Vite, HYG v3.7, live at bobmap.pixelmatter.org — and it is prettier than ours. Do NOT answer it with Three.js. Ours is already a real 3D chart: measured coordinates, orthographic projection, drag-rotate, depth cueing, SVG for crisp labels and click targets over a canvas backdrop of 3,005 stars. Vendoring 600KB of someone else's engine to get glow would triple the page and put the largest single body of code in the project outside our own review, in a project whose whole argument is that everything here is checkable.

The shine is framing and light, not an engine. Three changes get most of it: a perspective divide instead of the current orthographic scale; additive glow on the star sprites, which canvas 2D does natively with radial gradients and lighter compositing; and — the actual idea — bound the volume. A holotank is a tank. Ours fills its pane edge to edge like a diagram; give it a floor grid, corner brackets and a plinth line and it reads as a thing sitting on Bill's desk rather than a chart filling a window. Label it [HOLOTANK]. That is the canon word, checked: 34 hits, and holosphere has none.

items.text: Make the suites fail closed
items.note:
Deriving expectations from data/*.json instead of hardcoding them was the right fix and it has a blind spot in it: a case that computes an expected count of zero and observes zero passes without proving anything happened. A bug that empties a register would sail straight through, and the suite would report it as a pass in the same cheerful tone as everything else. Assert the critical lists are non-empty before comparing them. We have already lost most of a day to a harness that kept saying 2,585 checks passed while the books themselves were sitting deleted on disk; this is that shape again, drawn smaller.

Done, in two layers. `each(label, items, fn)` and `need(label, value)` in the harness fail when a collection is empty or a lookup finds nothing, instead of iterating zero times and reporting success; and a per-suite check floor in tests/__snapshots__/checks.json, recorded like the golden master, fails any suite that runs materially fewer assertions than it did when the count was last set on purpose. The first guards the sites that use it, the second catches the class. Verified by emptying a register in the built page: both fired, the floor reporting blog down from 150 checks to 6.

The audit itself found the legibility suite asserting almost nothing. Its WCAG contrast check looked up --bg and --ink, neither of which has ever been in the stylesheet — the background is --void — so it hit `continue` on every pass and never ran once, in the suite written because --ash was found at 2.26:1. Its spectral-colour check matched class="star-body", which the chart has never emitted. 8 checks became 147, and two real failures fell out: .statusbar .keys and .star.future .star-label were painting text in --rule at 2.41:1. Both are --ash now. The check was rewritten to walk every CSS rule that paints text rather than a hand-kept list of colours.

items.text: In Memorium built, and it caught two records that were flatly wrong
items.note: Four named Bobs are confirmed beyond recovery — Arthur (booby trap, no backup existed), Milo (transfer cut off mid-send), Homer (his own reactor, after deleting every backup he had) and Gerry (deleted by his own clones). Three more entries are counted and unnamed: Bill totted up three failed transfers among the six vessels lost at 82 Eridani and never said which, so the list carries three rows that can never be filled in. Nine more sit unaccounted, ships destroyed and backups never mentioned again. The old three-value status had no way to say 'destroyed and came back', so it said lost — about Elmer, who Bill confirms made it four paragraphs later, and about Bender, whose recovery is the entire plot of book 4. Taylor spells it In Memorium and validate.py now fails the build if anyone corrects it.

items.text: The eight unaccounted — is any of them settled somewhere we haven't looked
items.note:
Swept, and the answer is no. Every chapter after each loss was searched for the name — the method that moved Hannibal out of presumed when he turned up commanding a squad seventy-two years later. None of the eight comes back. The appendices were checked separately, since they carry no date and a date filter skips them; the printed genealogy lists three of these Bobs as parentage and says nothing about any fate.

Every later hit was somebody else, and those are worth keeping so nobody re-runs this and gets excited: Tom is Tom Cruise and later Tom Sawyer, Jackson is Peter Jackson, Barney is a Quinlan hotel called Barney's Place. Fred is a Deltan hunter from Bk2 ch1 who becomes an antagonist through book 3. Hector is Hector Rodriguez, a human, in Bk5 ch33 and ch45 — and separately the eighteenth-generation Bob who emails Bill in Bk5 ch38, already on file. Jeffrey is the Deltan council leader, which was already written down.

The starkest part is the quiet: Jackson, Milton and Zeke are each named exactly once in five books, in the chapter where they are lost, and Barney twice counting the printed genealogy. The register says so now. The three blank rows stay drawn from five; the arithmetic does not close from this end, and nothing found here suggests it ever will without a new source.

items.text: Taylor's genealogy is printed in the books — 18 promoted
items.note: The tree dropped as 'Taylor's 2017 genealogy' is an appendix in book 2, reprinted in book 4. Back matter, exactly like the Cast of Characters, which had already been supplying tier-T parentages for ten records. It agrees with all 26 parentages the narrative had given us, contradicts none, names no Bob we lack a record for, and settled the 18 whose priorClaim read 'the books don't say so'. Promoted, cited Bk2 · Genealogy. Tier C went 51 to 33, tier T 32 to 50, cited 52 to 70, and traces reaching Bob-1 went 34 to 52. It also settled a second question nobody asked: the printed tree is not the online one — where the online tree spelled Jonny 'Johnny' and Jacques 'Jaques', the appendix matches the narrative. The 12 wiki leads stand unchanged.

items.text: Sweeps re-run against the appendices
items.note: Every sweep this project ran was blind to the back matter. Re-run: the List of Terms expands FAITH — Free American Independent Theocratic Hegemony — which the register had recorded as a deliberate gap on the grounds that the books never unpack it. They do, in an appendix. Mention counts were refreshed and now exclude appendices by design, since an alphabetical cast list names everyone once and would flatten the ordering the registers sort on; that also caught two stale figures sitting inside the validator tolerance, hydra 4 to 1 and humans 512 to 497. The Cast of Characters names none of the nine unaccounted, so it does not settle them. The peoples suite no longer asserts that FAITH has no expansion — it checks that every expansion appears somewhere in the corpus, which is the rule the FAITH assertion was a special case of.

items.text: Notes audited for claims about what the books don't say
items.note: 33 absence-phrases across 27 records. Most are correct and stay: the pigoid really never learns, Bridget really had never seen a trout, and 'the books never say which three' was verified by an exhaustive sweep this morning. Two things came out. The twelve remaining wiki leads all carried the sentence that was wrong eighteen times — 'The books don't say so' — rewritten to distinguish not found from does not exist. And the audit caught a live bug it had not been looking for: five fateNotes restated the pool arithmetic in prose, and all three figures had gone stale within hours, because Elmer's vessel turned out to be the seventh and Hannibal was ruled out the same day. The arithmetic now lives in memorium.json alone and the register derives the rest; validate.py rejects a pooled candidate whose note restates it. Same rule as gen: store a number only where it can't be derived.

items.text: Publish it
items.note: Done. Live at ashestoaltar.github.io/bobiverse-companion, and on the custom domain as well. Two things stood in the way that the workflow could not do for itself: Pages had never been switched on for the repository, and the workflow's own token is not allowed to switch it on — enabled from the CLI, with enablement:true left in the workflow so a fork with a permissive token needs no steps at all. The LICENSE split and the self-contained check were already in place. Before flipping public, `make scan-history` checked every version of every publishable file and every commit message for book text; it found two historical fragments, both since paraphrased away or moot, and the decision to publish as-is was the owner's.

items.text: Spoiler gating, stolen from thunfischtoast/bobiverse-map
items.note: Done, and it grew well past a filter. READ THROUGH BOOK N, asked once on the way in and addressable as ?b=. Three things gate separately because they spoil at different rates: whether a record exists, by the earliest book it is cited from; its fate, by fateCite; and our prose, by a declared `spoil` — down to the paragraph, because four of Homer's five fate paragraphs are the book he dies in and only the fifth is the coda. Also gated: factions, which are book 4; names, since Riker is not Will until Bk3 ch57; multi-part citations; filters; search; sorting; and the chip row itself. Everything a record shows goes through one masking function so a field added later is held by default. tests/spoilers.test.js walks every register at every position looking for leaks and found seven that per-site gating had missed.

items.text: Mobile: second pass, the chart especially
items.note:
First pass, on a real phone, found three things. The shell is position:fixed with one grid row doing all the scrolling, so in landscape the furniture ate the whole 390px, the scrolling row collapsed and nothing scrolled at all — below 860px wide or 560px tall it is now an ordinary scrolling document. The register table was width:100% with ellipsised cells, so there was nothing to side-scroll to; it now sets its own width inside a wrapper. And the chart offered three gestures a phone cannot make, now rewritten for multiple pointers: one finger rotates, two pinch and pan, a star selects on release if the gesture travelled under eight pixels.

Then the chart stopped rendering entirely, which was self-inflicted and worth remembering: .chart-stage is flex:1 for the desktop layout, flex:1 sets flex-basis:0, and in a column flex container the basis beats height on the main axis — so the height set for mobile did nothing and the stage was zero pixels tall. Fixed with flex:none, and confirmed on the phone.

The second pass has since fixed the defect that mattered most: the dossier was hidden unless state.selected was set, so on a phone the bestiary, peoples and every jump to a system built their dossier correctly and then hid it. Three of eight registers did nothing visible. Closing was broken the same way at every width. Both now ask the register through selOf(), and tests/mobile.test.js runs at 390px so the next phone-only rule cannot break in silence — every other suite runs at 1400px, where the sheet does not exist and the rule that hides it never executes. Also landed: the tab row scrolls rather than stacking, filters only appear where there is parentage to grade, a real doctype and head, theme-color, safe-area inset under the sheet, and a 16px search box so iOS stops zooming the page on focus.

The three open questions were then answered on the phone rather than argued about: touch-action:none does not trap the page, the labels survive decluttering at phone width, and the year scrubber is usable under a thumb. What is left of mobile is no longer a second pass but three ordinary items — the tree overflowing sideways, the sheet wanting a scrim and a thumb-sized close, and the chart repainting the whole sky on every pointer move.

items.text: Prior art surveyed on GitHub
items.note: About fifty Bobiverse repos. Star maps dominate, then timelines, then a few genealogies. The comparable ones: thunfischtoast/bobiverse-map (2D map and timeline, 19 systems, 50+ Bobs, chapter-gated for spoilers), Mikeda75/bobiverse-starmap (books 1-4, J2000 coordinates, guided camera tours), ruguevara/Bobmap (Three.js, HYG v3.7, ~110 stars, live), sbtn/treeofbob (D3, 47 Bobs, archived), eneko/Bobiverse (GraphViz). Most-starred thing in the whole ecosystem is OpenGUPPIE, a physical Guppy build, at 24. Two findings worth keeping. Not one of them cites the text — thunfischtoast tags chapters but for spoiler gating, not provenance, and nobody anywhere distinguishes stated from inferred or records what is unknown. And they are all downstream of the same secondary source: treeofbob cites a 2017 PDF at kurt-anderson.com, which is almost certainly the tree this project dropped, and which we now know differs from the genealogy printed in book 2. The ecosystem is building on a copy while the original is in the back of the book.

items.text: The chart rebuilds itself on every pointer move
items.note:
paintChart() rewrites the whole SVG through innerHTML and repaints the five thousand star backdrop on every pointermove, which on a phone is a repaint per frame of a drag for a scene that has not changed except for its camera. Throttle to requestAnimationFrame, and consider thinning or skipping the backdrop while a gesture is in flight — the sky is the expensive half and nobody reads it mid-rotate. Worth measuring before assuming it is a problem; the phone renders it, the question is what it costs to move it.

Done, and measured first as the note asked. The premise was wrong in one detail — the 5,070-star backdrop is already on a canvas, not in the SVG — but the cost was real: 5.27ms of per-frame work on a desktop before any draw calls, and a phone is several times slower than that. Three causes. A star's colour, brightness and size are properties of the star and cannot change when the camera moves, yet were being recomputed every frame: 2,668 ciColour() calls and 2,668 rgba strings thrown away sixty times a second to arrive at the same values, now done once in styleSky(). Assigning canvas.width reallocates the backing store even when the value is unchanged, so that is conditional now. And the continuous gestures — drag, wheel, year scrubber — coalesce through paintChartSoon(), because pointer events do not arrive at the refresh rate; a phone reports at 120Hz. 5.27ms to 3.18ms, with the allocations and the per-frame reallocation gone on top. paintChart() stays synchronous for render(), the resize hook and the tests.

items.text: The tree overflows sideways with nothing to scroll
items.note:
The register table learned this and the tree did not. .tree is white-space:pre, so a deep branch runs past the right edge of a phone with no way to reach it — the same bug the table had, which was fixed by giving it its own width inside a .scroll-x wrapper. Either do that, or tighten the indent per level below 860px. The tree is the one view where the horizontal axis carries meaning, so cutting it off is worse here than anywhere else.

Done. .tree had no width of its own, so a white-space:pre block overflowed its own box silently — the scroll container above saw a child exactly as wide as itself and offered nothing to scroll. width:max-content with min-width:100% inside a .scroll-x wrapper, the same shape the register table got. Kept the indent rather than tightening it below 860px: the horizontal axis is the descent, so compressing it would cost the meaning the view exists to show.

items.text: The dossier sheet is a panel wearing a sheet's position
items.note:
On a phone it is fixed over a scrolling document with no scrim behind it, no scroll lock under it and no tap-outside to dismiss — so the page keeps scrolling beneath a thing that looks modal, and the only way out is a 24px close button against the ~44px that thumbs actually want. It is also 64dvh over a chart that is 58dvh, which is two numbers that were chosen separately. Wants: a scrim, overflow locked while open, a bigger close target, and one decision about how tall it is.

Done. The three omissions were one: it looked modal and was not. There is a scrim that exists only at sheet widths, a scroll lock on the body, and a 40px close target in place of 24 — which matters because there is no Escape key on a phone, so the button and focus are the only ways out. All three are set in syncSheet() rather than at the click, because the sheet opens and closes without one: a link arriving with a selection, a resize across the breakpoint, a reading position dropping the record that was open. The two heights that had been picked separately, 64dvh and 58dvh, are now one --sheet.

items.text: Focus goes nowhere in particular
items.note:
The tab bar has role=tablist but no aria-controls and no roving tabindex, so arrow keys do not move between tabs the way a tablist promises they will. Opening a dossier does not move focus into it and closing one does not put focus back on the row that opened it, which on a keyboard means every close drops you at the top of the document. On a phone it matters more than it looks: with Escape unavailable, focus and the close button are the only ways out.

Done. The tab bar claimed role=tablist and did not implement one, which is worse than never claiming it — a screen reader promises the reader arrow keys and nothing happens. It has aria-controls, a roving tabindex so the bar is one tab stop rather than ten, and Left/Right/Home/End with the view following focus. Closing a dossier returns focus to the row that opened it; since render() rewrites the stage, what is remembered is the selector rather than the node, because the element is gone by the time anyone closes it. An opening sheet takes focus, but only on the transition — re-taking it every render would fight anybody typing in the search box with a record open — and a desktop dossier never takes it at all, being a column that was already there. The DOM stub had focus() as a no-op, so none of this was observable; it records activeElement now, and tests/focus.test.js is the suite.

items.text: The boot sequence is a mainframe, and the books describe a SCUT connect
items.note:
Done. The books show a first SCUT connect twice and agree — Riker in Bk1 ch41, Mulder in Bk2 ch6. Turn it on; the console lists the systems already on the network; work the menus and register yourself; pick one and connect; the transmitting icon comes up; the far end answers. Nobody mounts anything. The sequence now reads that way and ends where it always did, on STATUS: Ready.

The four systems it offers are derived — earliest contacted, in order — and come out as Epsilon Eridani, Omicron² Eridani, Sol and Alpha Centauri, which is the same four the books print on Mulder's console. Being able to check that rather than assert it is the whole reason to derive it. Every figure is still read from the data, and a test now rejects the words a mainframe would use.

Two lines longer than before at the same six seconds, so BOOT_SPEED came down: a handshake should read briskly and the part worth reading is what the archive says it holds. On a touch screen the hint says TAP rather than naming a key nobody has.

items.text: Write down that look-and-feel is always local
items.note: Already written, and had been before this item was raised — CLAUDE.md has carried it under what the books establish about BobNet. There is no BobNet lobby and no house style: connecting means standing inside somebody else's VR, an undecorated one is a bare blue room, and the Moot VR gets reconfigured per occasion. Which is what makes the amber console legitimate rather than invented: canon is consistent that presentation is personal. It is also, in the end, why the CRT overlay came out — the styling is Bill's room, and his room did not need scanlines to be his.

items.text: Two Bobs are wearing names they have not taken yet
items.note: Done. `nameFrom` records the chapter a Bob took the name we file him under — Bk3 ch57 for Will, Bk4 ch3 for Morlock — and it is a citation rather than a number, so the same check that verifies every other citation against the corpus verifies this one. Below that book the console calls him by his alias and drops the second name entirely: at book one he is Riker in the register, in the tree, in the trace, and in Homer's SOURCE BOB column. It folds into shown(), so it reached all of those at once. The validator now errors on an alias with no nameFrom, since that combination is exactly the bug this fixed.

items.text: Book 6 — the release-day procedure
items.note:
The Infinite Extent is out 10 Sept 2026. The console no longer hardcodes how long the series is: data/books.json is the one place, and the entry for book 6 is already there with released:false. Release day is flip that boolean, add the ebook to books/, `make corpus`, `make validate`, `make snapshots`, `make build`. The flag is stored rather than compared against today's date on purpose — a date comparison would change the rendered page overnight and break the golden master with nobody having touched anything.

The validator will refuse the build until every corpus-bounded claim has been re-checked, which is the next item and is deliberately in the way. Expect the reading position to gain BOOK 6 and the prompt to say six; both derive, and tests/books.test.js fails if either stops deriving. Taylor has said seven will be the last, so this happens once more after that.

items.text: Re-check the five corpus-bounded claims against book 6
items.note:
Five sentences on the page are not counts but findings, and their scope is the corpus that was searched: that nobody in five books goes back to which three transfers failed; that the Bobs spend five books arguing over who counts as a person; that Jackson, Milton and Zeke are each named exactly once; that mention counts span the five books; and the register's own note saying the same of the quiet three. A new book does not leave those true by having the number incremented — if book 6 returns to any of it, the claim is simply wrong, and renumbering would launder it into a bigger lie.

So they are registered in validate.py's CORPUS_CLAIMS with the book count each was established against, and the build fails on every one of them the day the series grows. Re-read, then either re-establish against six, re-bound to what was actually searched, or withdraw. This is the failure this project has already paid for once: priorClaim boilerplate asserted the books were silent about eighteen parentages that book 2's appendix states outright.

items.text: Re-sweep the open questions against book 6
items.note:
The first new evidence this project has had since it started. Worth doing as one pass rather than piecemeal, and worth not starting any of it before the book is read — several of these are exactly the kind of debt an author pays off late in a series.

In order of how much a single sentence could settle: the three blank In Memorium rows, still drawn from five; the eight unaccounted, swept once and null; Marcus's parentage, ten POV chapters and no source; Thor, Jeffrey, Milton and Zeke; the Hector collision; and the twelve remaining wiki leads. Also re-run the biographical sweep — 17 birth dates and 3 vessels came out for want of a citation and a sixth book may put some back.

Note that ingesting book 6 invalidates every mention count in the bestiary and peoples registers at the same time, since those are re-derived from the corpus. That is the check working, not a regression.

items.text: How long the series is, said once
items.note:
BOOK_MAX was a literal 5 in the template, BOOKS was a literal 5 in the validator, and four rendered sentences counted the books by hand. data/books.json is now the only place that knows, and the console, the reading-position selector, the spoiler prompt and the validator's bounds all derive from it. Done four weeks before book 6 rather than on the day, because the day it matters is the day you least want to be restructuring a constant across three layers — and every mistake would ship to exactly the people arriving for the new book.

The distinction that took the thinking: a count is arithmetic and belongs to the data, so it renders from BOOK_MAX and cannot drift, while a claim about what the books do or do not contain is a finding whose scope is the corpus searched. Pattern-matching English cannot tell them apart — 'his fate runs across three books' and 'nobody in five books ever goes back to it' are the same shape and opposite things. So the claims are registered by hand and the counts are rendered. Output byte-identical: 132 snapshot states unchanged.

items.text: Species portraits, and the Others described after all
items.note:
Five plates for the peoples register — humans, Deltans, Quinlans, Pav, the Others — at 16:10 instead of the bestiary's 4:3, head and shoulders with the eyes front instead of a side profile. The difference is deliberate and load-bearing: validate.py already refuses to let one name sit in both registers, because the series is Bob working out who counts as a person and filing the Deltans under beasts would make the console argue the opposite. A drawing makes that argument too. A side profile is a specimen laid out for measurement; a portrait looks back.

Grounded in the text rather than invented. Deltans: bat ears, short snout, fur, long thin limbs (Bk2 ch65). Quinlans: the Bobs arguing in front of the image at Bk4 ch8 — otter, flying squirrel, giant beaver — settling on a four-foot otter with a skin flap along the forearm, a snout close to a beak but toothed, and a fanning tail. Pav: giant meerkats, six feet upright, quadrupedal over distance, furry (Bk2 ch63-64).

The Others were nearly a null result and should not have been. Five corpus sweeps came back empty and the register briefly carried a note saying no physical description was on record. It was wrong: Bk2 ch57 has Bill presenting composite scan images to the moot and talking the room through the anatomy for a page and a half, which makes it the most detailed description of any species in the books. The sweeps missed it because every pattern looked for the plural name beside anatomy words in the same sentence, and the passage uses 'the Other', 'the creature', 'the thing', with the anatomy spread across dialogue. A description is a passage, not a sentence. Five failures of one bad method read as corroboration rather than as one mistake repeated — which is the exact trap the no-source-found rule exists to catch, sprung by the person who wrote it down.

The nine polities stay dashed. A government is not a thing you draw, and FAITH does not even get its acronym expanded because nobody in the books unpacks it; an invented emblem would be a larger fabrication than an invented meaning.

items.text: System map
items.note:
Built, as a peer register at #systems. It owns no data — origin, lostAt and visited on the records, `system` on a creature or a people, and the astrometry already in systems.json — which is the In Memorium shape again rather than a new file.

It does three things the chart cannot. It is a list, so places can be read rather than hunted for among overlapping dots. It answers a search, which the chart ignores entirely. And it holds Trantor and Jabberwocky, the two systems with no coordinates, which a star map can only mention in a footnote because there is nowhere to draw a megastructure with no parallax.

The tie mark is the honest part and the reason the register is worth having: filled for a place a record names, half for one only narrated from, hollow for one in the file for its astrometry alone. It moves with the reading position — seven named by a record at book one, fifteen at the end — and it turns the thinness of `visited` into something visible instead of something you would have to go looking for.

The dossier is the chart's, not a second copy. The timeline's rule for how late a place may date itself was factored into datedHorizon() so both registers read the same one; two copies of a rule that fiddly drift the first time either is edited.
